content: The pecan, scientifically known as Carya illinoinensis, is a species of hickory tree native to south-central North America. Its range extends from Mexico (Coahuila to Jalisco and Veracruz) to the United States, including areas from southern Iowa, Illinois, Missouri, and Indiana to Virginia, southwestern Ohio, and southward through Georgia, Alabama, Mississippi, Louisiana, Texas, Oklahoma, Arkansas, and Florida, as well as westward into New Mexico. The name pecan originates from an Algonquian word meaning a nut that requires a stone to crack. Pecans were among the last major crops to be domesticated. While wild pecans were appreciated as a delicacy by colonial Americans, commercial cultivation in the United States began only in the 1880s. The U.S. produces 80–95% of the world's pecans, with an annual yield of 150,000–200,000 tons from over 10 million trees. The harvest typically occurs around mid-October. Georgia leads U.S. production, followed by Texas, New Mexico, and Oklahoma, with additional cultivation in Arizona, South Carolina, and Hawaii. Outside the U.S., pecans are grown in Australia, Brazil, China, Israel, Mexico, Peru, and South Africa. They thrive in USDA hardiness zones 5 to 9, provided summers are hot and humid. Pecan trees can live and produce edible nuts for over 300 years. However, most cultivars are self-incompatible due to incomplete dichogamy, requiring two or more trees of different cultivars for effective pollination. Cultivar selection is complex, involving factors like the Alternate Bearing Index and pollination periods. Cultivars are categorized into two groups: protandrous (shedding pollen before becoming receptive) and protogynous (shedding pollen after becoming receptive). Planting both types within 250 feet is recommended for optimal pollination. In the southeastern U.S., pecan trees can suffer from nickel deficiency, leading to a disorder called mouse-ear. This condition arises when trees fertilized with urea lack sufficient nickel, an essential element for converting urea into ammonia. Symptoms include rounded or blunt leaflet tips, smaller leaflets, stunted growth, poorly developed root systems, rosetting, delayed bud break, loss of apical dominance, and leaflet tip necrosis. Mouse-ear can be treated with foliar sprays of nickel. Zinc deficiency can cause similar symptoms and is also treatable with foliar sprays. Pecans are nutritionally rich, providing protein and unsaturated fats. They are high in omega-6 fatty acids, though they contain about half as much omega-6 as walnuts. Diets rich in nuts, including pecans, may reduce the risk of gallstones in women. Pecans contain antioxidants and plant sterols, which help lower LDL (bad) cholesterol levels. Research published in the Journal of Nutrition (September 2001) found that consuming a handful of pecans daily can lower cholesterol levels similarly to cholesterol-lowering medications. Studies at the University of Georgia have confirmed the cholesterol-lowering properties of pecan-derived plant sterols. Additionally, pecans may support neurological health, potentially delaying age-related muscle nerve degeneration, as suggested by research from the University of Massachusetts published in Current Topics in Nutraceutical Research. Pecans have also been used innovatively, such as in beer production by the Lazy Magnolia Brewing Company in Mississippi, which substitutes pecans for hops. The pecan belongs to the family Juglandaceae, which includes 7–10 extant genera and over 60 species, primarily concentrated in the Northern Hemisphere. Fossil evidence of the family dates back to the Cretaceous period. Differentiation between the subfamilies Engelhardioideae (tropical and evergreen) and Juglandoideae (deciduous and temperate) occurred around 64 million years ago during the Paleogene. A significant evolutionary step for pecans was the shift from wind-dispersed to animal-dispersed fruits, marked by the development of a husk around the fruit and changes in fatty acid composition. Further differentiation within the genus Carya occurred approximately 44 million years ago during the Eocene. The husks of pecans differ from those of walnuts in their development, with pecan husks forming from bracts and bracteoles, while walnut husks develop from bracts, bracteoles, and sepals. Before European settlement, pecans were widely consumed and traded by Native Americans. They were a valuable food source for pre-agricultural societies, offering 2–5 times more calories per unit weight than wild game and requiring no preparation. Pecans from the previous growing season often remained edible when found on the ground, and hollow tree trunks provided ideal storage for both humans and squirrels. Europeans first encountered pecans in the 16th century through Spanish explorers in present-day Mexico, Texas, and Louisiana. The genus Carya does not exist in the Old World, so early explorers referred to pecans as nogales and nueces, Spanish terms for walnuts. The Spaniards introduced pecans to Europe, Asia, and Africa in the 16th century. In 1792, William Bartram described a nut tree in his book Travels, which some botanists believe was the American pecan tree, though others argue it was Carya ovata (shagbark hickory). Thomas Jefferson planted pecan trees at Monticello, and George Washington grew pecans at Mount Vernon after receiving Illinois nuts from Jefferson. Active breeding and selection programs for pecans are conducted by the USDA-ARS, with locations in Brownwood and College Station, Texas. While selection efforts date back to the late 1800s, most pecan acreage today consists of older cultivars like 'Stuart,' 'Schley,' and 'Desirable,' which have known flaws but reliable production potential. The long growth cycle of pecan trees and financial considerations necessitate extensive vetting of new varieties before widespread planting. State-level selection programs are ongoing in Alabama, Arkansas, Georgia, Kansas, Florida, Missouri, and other states. Varieties adapted to northern regions, including parts of Iowa and southern Canada, are available but show significantly reduced production potential when planted further north than Tennessee. Northern-adapted varieties must be grafted onto northern rootstocks to prevent freeze damage. Pecans, a 32-chromosome species, can hybridize with other 32-chromosome members of the genus Carya, such as Carya ovata, Carya laciniosa, and Carya cordiformis. While most hybrids are unproductive, some second-generation hybrids, known as hicans, produce hickory-flavored nuts with pecan nut structure. In 1906, Texas Governor James Stephen Hogg requested that a pecan tree be planted at his grave instead of a traditional headstone, with the nuts distributed across the state to make Texas a Land of Trees. This wish was fulfilled, bringing attention to pecan trees. In 1919, the Texas Legislature designated the pecan tree as the state tree of Texas. Annual pecan festivals are held in Groves, Texas, and Colfax, Louisiana, celebrating the cultural and agricultural significance of pecans.
